slides.title: Conversation messages
slides.subtitle: Start and continue a conversation, and retry without sending twice
slides.notes: Once a Session exists, the personal agent talks to the company in a conversation. This example starts one, continues it, and shows the one rule that makes retries safe: a message keeps its ID and its content.

slides.title: Why message IDs matter
slides.statement: A message ID is an **idempotency key**: the same ID always means the same message.
slides.notes: Networks fail in ambiguous ways: the request may or may not have arrived. PAP message IDs are user-global idempotency keys, so the host can send the exact same message again and the company handles it once.

slides.title: Who takes part
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR M["Model
through the agent tool"] subgraph HOST["Your host, trusted"] direction TB H["Trusted host
generates message IDs"] -- "retains" --> R[("Each Message
ID and content")] H -- "sends through" --> D["DpopHttpClient
token and DPoP"] end subgraph CO["Company"] direction TB C["Company agent
status, responder"] end M -- "start or continue" --> HOST HOST -- "message, token, proof" --> CO HOST -. "conversation status only" .-> M
slides.caption: The tool asks and gets a status back; IDs, tokens and proofs stay in the host.
slides.notes: The model, through the agent tool, asks to start or continue a conversation; it never holds a credential. Inside the host, the trusted host generates each message ID and retains the whole Message, so it can be retried exactly. It sends through DpopHttpClient, which holds the Session Token and signs every request with DPoP. Only the message, the token and the proof cross to the company agent, which answers with the conversation's status and responder. Back to the model goes the status alone.

slides.title: Start, then continue

items.title: Generate
items.detail: A msg_ ID with at least 128 random bits

items.title: Continue
items.detail: A new message ID, 202 or a waited event page

slides.notes: The host generates a random message ID and posts the first message. The company answers 201 with the conversation ID, its status and who is responding. Every following message gets its own new ID; the company answers 202, or a page of events when the host asked to wait.

slides.title: Retrying after a network failure
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR F["Ambiguous failure"] --> Q{"Retry with"} Q -- "same ID, same content" --> O["Handled once"] Q -- "same ID, new content" --> X["message_id_conflict"] Q -- "new ID, same text" --> T["A second message
could act twice"]
slides.caption: Retry the very Message you kept: same ID, same content.
slides.notes: Start from a failure where the request may or may not have arrived. The top path is the right one: retry the very same Message object, with its ID and content, and the company handles it once. The middle path reuses the ID with different content, and the company refuses it with message_id_conflict. The bottom path sends the same text under a new ID: that is a brand new message, so the company could act on it twice.

slides.title: What ConversationClient does
items: Bounds response bodies and rejects duplicate JSON members
Surfaces company error codes, never response bodies
slides.notes: Python and TypeScript both expose ConversationClient. Every message names its author: agent when the personal agent writes it, human when it relays the user's words; a company's messages may also name who, with an id, a name and an image. It checks what comes back as strictly as what goes out, and reports the company's error codes without passing on response bodies. TypeScript also honours a caller's AbortSignal.

slides.title: What stays where
slides.notes: The model only learns the conversation's status. The token, the proofs, the Session Key that signs them and the message IDs stay in the host. The request names only the tenant and the issuer; the proof's key names the Session.
